units.text: INT. RIDESHARE CAR - NIGHT
The Corolla smells of pine air freshener and old fries.
The dashboard clock says 2:04 and the wipers drag across a windshield that is barely wet, a drizzle that cant decide to become rain.
Mo has been driving eleven hours.
He keeps the radio low, some call-in show about gardening, because silence in this car has a way of getting loud.
The back door opens.
A woman folds herself into the seat behind him with a duffel bag held against her chest like something that might be taken from her.
She does not say hello.
She is maybe forty, her coat is too light for the season, and there is a smear of dried mascara she hasnt noticed or has stopped caring about.
Fourteen Alder Court.
units.name: THE WOMAN

units.text: That's what the app says. You're, uh, Rhea?
units.name: MO

units.text: Whatever it says.
units.name: THE WOMAN

units.text: He checks the mirror.

She is looking out of the window at nothing, at the shuttered laundromat and the one bright gas station, and he recognises the look, he has seen it on fathers outside delivery rooms and on men outside courtrooms.
It is the look of someone rehearsing.
He pulls out.
The gardening show talks about slugs.
Long night?
units.name: MO

units.text: Don't do that.
units.name: THE WOMAN

units.text: Do what?
units.name: MO

units.text: The thing where you're nice so I'll talk. I'm paying for a ride. Not a conversation.
units.name: THE WOMAN

units.text: He lets that sit.
In the mirror her jaw works.
She unzips the duffel an inch, looks inside, zips it again.
It is a small movement and he files it away the way he files away everything, the plates that linger behind him, the bars that empty out at the wrong time.
Twelve years of this has made him a reluctant expert in other peoples bad nights.
Okay. Radio's yours if you want it.
units.name: MO

units.text: She doesn't want it.
The car rolls under a yellow light that blinks and blinks for no one.
Is it far? From here.
units.name: THE WOMAN

units.text: Nine minutes. Maybe ten.
units.name: MO

units.text: Can you make it twelve.
units.name: THE WOMAN

units.text: He glances back.
She holds his eyes in the mirror for the first time and there is something so naked in it that he looks away first.
I can drive slow.
units.name: MO

units.text: Thank you.
units.name: THE WOMAN

units.text: He takes the long way along the river road.
Black water to the left, the shapes of warehouses to the right.
She counts something under her breath, streetlights maybe, or the days.
He cannot tell.
My daughter's about your age. Well. Younger. Twenty-six.
units.name: MO

units.text: I said not a conversation.
units.name: THE WOMAN

units.text: You did. Sorry.
units.name: MO

units.text: Does she call you?
units.name: THE WOMAN

units.text: He doesnt answer right away.
His thumb taps the wheel.
Sundays. Mostly.
units.name: MO

units.text: Mostly.
units.name: THE WOMAN

units.text: Mostly.
units.name: MO

units.text: She nods slowly, as if he has confirmed a theory.
Then her phone lights up in her lap and she flinches like it burned her.
She turns it face down.
It lights up again through her fingers, a pale glow around the edges of her hand, and again, and she presses her whole palm over it.
You can pick up. I don't mind.
units.name: MO

units.text: It's my brother.
units.name: THE WOMAN

units.text: Bad news kind of brother?
units.name: MO

units.text: The kind that's right.
units.name: THE WOMAN

units.text: That lands somewhere in him.
He slows for no reason at an empty crosswalk.
He said don't come. He said she wouldn't want it. Our mother. That after nine years she's not going to want me standing in her hallway at two in the morning with a bag.
units.name: THE WOMAN

units.text: Is that what's in the bag?
units.name: MO

units.text: Her things. What I took. I took a lot.
units.name: THE WOMAN

units.text: He nods like he understands, and it surprises him to find that he does, a little, that there is a version of him in a different car on a different night carrying a different bag up a different driveway.
The phone buzzes again.
She finally turns it over and reads and her face does something complicated.
He says the porch light's on.
units.name: THE WOMAN

units.text: Is that good?
units.name: MO

units.text: She leaves it on every night. He says she always has. Since I left.
units.name: THE WOMAN

units.text: She laughs, one cracked note, and then she is crying, quietly and efficiently, the way people cry who have practiced it alone in cars.
He keeps his eyes on the road.
He reaches across and pulls a napkin from the glovebox without looking and holds it back between the seats.
She takes it.
Rhea's not my name. It's my sisters. I use hers on the app.
units.name: THE WOMAN

units.text: Okay.
units.name: MO

units.text: It's Tamsin. I'm Tamsin.
units.name: THE WOMAN

units.text: I'm Mo.
units.name: MO

units.text: I know. It says on the app. Your picture's older than you.
units.name: TAMSIN

units.text: It's from a better year.
units.name: MO

units.text: She almost smiles.
The river road bends away from the water and the houses start, porch after porch, dark windows and sleeping cars.
Alder Court is two turns ahead and they both know it.
He takes the first turn very slowly.
What if I get out and I can't walk to the door.
units.name: TAMSIN

units.text: Then you sit in the car a while. The meter's not running. I'll say it's broke.
units.name: MO

units.text: Is it broke?
units.name: TAMSIN

units.text: It's whatever you need it to be.
units.name: MO

units.text: He turns onto Alder Court.
Number fourteen is a narrow house with green shutters and, over the door, a single yellow bulb, burning, with moths turning around it like slow thoughts.
He stops the car a little short of it and puts it in park.
The engine ticks.
The gardening man says goodnight.
She does not move.
He does not make her.
Her hand finds the door handle and rests there, and for a long time that is all that happens in the car, two people and a yellow light, until upstairs in the house a curtain shifts.
Oh god. She's up.
units.name: TAMSIN

units.text: Maybe she never went to bed.
units.name: MO

units.text: Tamsin picks up the duffel.
Her hands are shaking so badly the zipper rattles.
She opens the door and the cold comes in and the drizzle, finally, begins to be rain.
Wait here? Just till I'm inside.
units.name: TAMSIN

units.text: I'll wait till the light goes off. Or you tell me to go.
units.name: MO

units.text: She steps out.
She looks at the house.
Then she leans back down to the window, rain on her face, and for a second she looks about twenty, a girl in a doorway of her own making.
Five stars.
units.name: TAMSIN

units.text: Go on.
units.name: MO

units.text: She goes up the path.

The front door opens before she reaches it and a small gray figure stands in the yellow light with one hand over her mouth, and Mo, who has seen a lot of doors, looks away to give them the dignity of it, and turns the radio off.
